summary.title: The Death of Microservice Madness in 2018
summary.one_liner: Microservices bring real benefits in independent development, deployment and scaling, but they add hard costs in operations, state, versioning, transactions and networking, so adopt them only after weighing those trade-offs.
takeaways: Microservices offer independent development, deployment, scaling and reuse, but these benefits weaken when service boundaries are poorly defined.
State, schema changes and message queues make rolling out services together hard; stateless services are much easier to handle.
Distributed transactions, retries and versioning across live services are major sources of difficulty.
Running an orchestration platform such as Kubernetes adds significant operational and networking complexity, even with managed services.
Microservices are a packaging and operations pattern rather than an architecture; boundary design remains the core engineering challenge.
summary.summary: The author argues against 'microservice madness', the assumption that adopting microservices automatically brings devops success. He first sets out the benefits of splitting a hypothetical video platform into independent services, then walks through the main challenges: developer and operator complexity, the need for expertise, poorly defined boundaries, state and schema, inter-service communication, versioning, distributed transactions, managing the cluster, and networking. The article closes with a set of self-assessment questions (in a linked PDF) and the point that microservices are not themselves an architecture.
